archetype.name: Gunslinger (now a short-yardage backup)
archetype.definition: A veteran thrower who lives on aggressive downfield throws and accepts interceptions, sacks and inaccuracy as the price. He has been benched for J.J. McCarthy and now gets snaps mainly as a sneak and designed-run option.

report.headline: Four starts of classic Winston chaos, then the bench: deep juice, intermediate picks
report.take:
Jameis Winston took over from Jaxson Dart after a Week 2 relief outing and started Weeks 3 through 6. As of November 3 he is the QB2 behind J.J. McCarthy. The four-start sample looked like the rest of his career. He was willing to throw into tight windows and the ball came out wild. His bad-throw rate of 23.4% ranks last among 38 charted passers. His CPOE of -8.94 ranks 43rd of 47. On his deep throws he still produced: +0.455 EPA per attempt on 23 throws of 20+ air yards. The season line of -0.117 EPA per dropback is the worst way to read him. The Week 2 relief game against the Rams (-16.5 EPA, 11 of 27) sinks it, and as a starter he sat at -0.026 per dropback. That is below the league's +0.034 but not a disaster.

The damage sits in the middle of the field and the intermediate zone. All five of his interceptions came on throws of 10-19 air yards, where he completed 46.2% at a CPOE of -10.3. Throws over the middle were his worst direction (-0.124 EPA, three picks). Add a pressure-to-sack rate of 38.5% (34th of 38) and you have the familiar Winston bargain: big plays deep and in the red zone, paid for by drive-killers. Career ranks show this is not new. His bad-throw rate ranked 44th or worse in every charted season since 2019, and his interception counts sat near the bottom of the league in the full-time years.

The benching followed his two-game swing. Week 5 at Washington was his best game (326 yards, three TDs, +10.6 EPA). Week 6 against New Orleans was the opposite: -12.0 EPA, two picks, a 30.8% bad-throw rate, and only 60% of the snaps. By Week 7 he played 8% of snaps, threw no passes, and ran four times with a rushing touchdown. That is his role now. The Giants use him under center in short yardage, where his 8 designed runs have gone for +0.7 EPA each and a 75% success rate despite 1.25 yards a carry.

Some of his numbers will not hold. The red-zone line of six TDs on 16 attempts with a +16.5 CPOE is far better than the rest of his accuracy profile, so it is the first thing that would regress if he played again. The deep EPA is more credible because it matches his whole career. Still, 23 attempts is a hint, not a fact. Unless McCarthy falters or gets hurt, Winston's weekly output is a handful of sneaks and the odd goal-line score.

strengths.title: Deep ball still produces
strengths.body: Throws of 20+ air yards produced +0.455 EPA per attempt and +10.5 EPA in total. That is the only depth band that clearly carried his passing. His CPOE there is close to neutral, so he is not simply getting lucky on low-probability throws. The aggression is career-long, and the deep value would likely return if he got snaps again, though 23 attempts is a thin base.

strengths.title: Short-yardage sneak and keeper value
strengths.body: His designed runs average only 1.25 yards, yet they post +0.7 EPA per play and a 75% success rate. They are third-and-short and goal-line conversions, which is exactly why the Giants kept him on the field in Week 7 after the benching. A 231-pound QB moving the chains is a sustainable niche, but it caps his volume at a few carries a game.

strengths.title: Red-zone and late-game finishing
strengths.body: He threw six TDs on 16 red-zone attempts at +0.513 EPA. He was also sharp in one-score fourth quarters (+0.354 EPA, 68.8% completions). Both are real moments, but both rest on fewer than 20 plays. His +16.5 red-zone CPOE is wildly out of line with his overall accuracy, so treat these as bonuses that will cool.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws became interception fuel
concerns.body: All five interceptions came on 10-19 yard throws. He completed 46.2% there at -10.3 CPOE, and the middle of the field was his worst area. This is the cost side of his aggression rather than a new flaw: his career interception ranks have long sat near the bottom of the league. It is why a run-first staff moved on.

concerns.title: Accuracy at the bottom of the league
concerns.body: A 23.4% bad-throw rate ranks dead last among charted passers. It fits a career in which he ranked 44th or worse in every charted season since 2019, including last of 63 in 2025. Shotgun dropbacks, the bulk of his work, sat at -0.147 EPA. Under center was close to average, which hints that play-action structure hid some of the inaccuracy. This is who he is, not a slump.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He turned 38.5% of pressures into sacks (34th of 38), with an 8.7% sack rate against a league average of 6.9%. His time to throw of 2.64 seconds is not long, so this is less about extending plays than holding for the big throw. The 2022 and 2024 seasons showed similar rates, so expect it to persist whenever he plays.

trend.note: His starts climbed from a punchless Week 3 to a strong Week 5 at Washington (+10.6 EPA). Week 6 collapsed into two picks and a partial benching at 60% of snaps, and by Week 7 he was a short-yardage specialist on 8% of snaps with no pass attempts.

nextGame.headline: Soft Eagles pass defense, but he's holding a clipboard
nextGame.body:
On paper Philadelphia is exactly the defense Winston would want. It ranks 29th in defensive EPA and 24th against the pass, and it is last in both hit rate and sack rate, which would ease his biggest weakness. It also allows 0.35 EPA per target to the lead tight end. The catch is that he is listed as QB2 behind McCarthy, so the matchup mostly matters if he enters the game. His realistic usage is a few sneaks and short-yardage keepers. Those gain value against a run defense ranked 31st in rush EPA, and the Giants are 3.5-point favorites with a 40.5 total, a script that should give them red-zone and third-and-short chances.

Availability on the Giants' side touches his role. Cam Skattebo is questionable with a hamstring and Tyrone Tracy Jr. is on IR. A thinner backfield could push more short-yardage carries to the quarterback package. Skattebo was also his best-performing target by EPA. On the Eagles' side, linebacker Jihaad Campbell (82% of snaps) is out, which weakens the middle of the field, both against the run and in the zone where Winston has struggled. Corners Jonathan Jones (out), Jakorian Bennett (IR) and Michael Carter II (questionable) are depth pieces rather than starters, so they matter little to his outlook.

keyMatchups.title: Eagles can't pressure the quarterback
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia ranks 32nd in both sack rate and hit rate. Winston's sack problem would be muted if he ended up dropping back, which makes him a more playable emergency option this week than most. It only matters if McCarthy leaves the game.

keyMatchups.title: Sneak package vs a leaky run defense
keyMatchups.body: The Eagles rank 31st in rush EPA, and Campbell's absence removes a high-snap linebacker. Winston's designed runs have been efficient conversions, so a couple of goal-line or third-and-short keepers are his likeliest contribution.

keyMatchups.title: Giants' backfield health
keyMatchups.body: Skattebo is a game-time decision and Tracy is on IR. That could tilt more short-yardage work toward the quarterback package, or remove the back who gave Winston +0.335 EPA per target as a passer. The reports are as of November 2 and are not final.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Giants keep using Winston in the red zone and on third-and-short, and how McCarthy's leash looks. Either is the only path back to real volume.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as McCarthy holds the job, expect Winston to play a small, specific role: a few designed runs and sneaks a game, rare pass attempts, and the occasional rushing touchdown that makes a week look better than it was. The skills behind that niche are size, the defense's need to respect the run, and a staff willing to use him. All of that is stable. Any passing work would be streaky. The deep-ball value is real across his career, but so are the intermediate interceptions, the bottom-of-the-league accuracy and the high sack rate. A run-first offense that passes far less than expected does not want that mix for long.

If he does return to starting through injury or a McCarthy slump, his starter line is the right baseline: roughly 200 yards a game with a touchdown and an interception, plus a few sacks. The red-zone efficiency would cool from its current level. The projections below assume the backup role, with the low end reflecting weeks he barely sees the field.

confidence.note: Role change to QB2 is clear, but his usage in the sneak package is one game old and depends on McCarthy's health and play.
